newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end sharply off on data, technicals.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end sharply off on data, technicals.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed sharply lower as the market tripped on expansionary economic data and key technical levels, players said.
The bellwether 30-year bond ended off 1-9/32 at 94-8/32. Its yield jumped to 7.09 percent, its highest closing level since 7.11 percent on September 11, 1996.
Losses eroded all sectors of the curve, including bills, which had racked up impressive gains on Wednesday.
Three-month T-bill rates backed up 3/32 to 5.23 percent, and the two-year note ended off 6/32 at 6.45 percent.

"Basically we got pasted by a very strong round of data, from jobless claims and mortgage applications to housing data and some of the proprietary inflation numbers," said Joe Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp.
Taken alone, any of the reports would have been of secondary importance. Together, however, they provided expansionary grist for the economic mill.
Among key releases, existing home sales rose 0.9 percent in February to an annual rate of 4.26 million units, higher than economists' average projection of 4.05 million.
PSA The Bond Market Trade Association recommended an early close for 1400 EST/1900 GMT Thursday and a full close Friday.

Traders said a large bank sold longer coupons after the 1000 EST/1500 GMT home sales report. That sent cash bonds and the June futures contract through key levels, prompting other dealers to follow suit, they said.
The bond yield climbed above 7.0 percent and the futures contract dropped below the equivalent 108-9/32.

"We had been bouncing around on either side of the 7.0-percent level, but today was the first time we really pushed decisively above there," said John Canavan, Treasury market analyst at Stone & McCarthy Research Associates Inc.
With 7.0 percent out of the way, several analysts agreed there was little technical support nearby.
"The next really solid top for the cash bond yield is 7.20 percent," Canavan said. "There isn't anything particularly strong before that."
That level held up through several tests in June and July, Canavan said.

A hefty load of new supply continued to weigh on the market Thursday. Throughout the week, $43.5 billion of one-, two- and five-year issues were auctioned, as well as $23.0 billion of three- and six-month bills.
"The dealers paid too much for twos and fives on Tuesday and Wednesday and there was no significant retail bid," CIBC's Liro said. "They're having a little bit of a fire sale."
Bills sold off on Thursday despite some experts' prediction they would continue to catch a bid from end-of-quarter reshuffling.
News reports that former Fed officials Lyle Gramley and Alan Blinder had said the central bank would likely tighten further to cool the economy affected the market little.
"I'm sure the Fed people aren't really making that much of a difference," said Matthew Alexy, Treasury market strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston.
More broadly, six-month bill rates ended up 3/32 at 5.36 percent, and yearbills closed up 6/32 at 5.69 percent.
The five-year note was off 18/32 at 99-11/32 to yield 6.78 percent, and the ten-year was off 28/32 at 95-10/32 to yield 6.91 percent.
